title: The France I Know, Now in Flames
author: Becky Grant
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/IMG_3364-680x510.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/30/the-
france-i-know-now-in-flames/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/IMG_3364-680x510.jpeg)

Cap Ferret peninsula, photo by Becky Grant.

If you think of France as a place to see the Eiffel Tower, sip wine, and eat
confit de canard or escargot in chic cafés with old zinc bars and woven café
chairs, you aren't entirely wrong. Those moments continue to exist, and
tourists can expect to find those same scenes in every wonderful
arrondissement; choose your favorite, just like you'd pick your pastry at the
pâtisserie… is it a pain au chocolat or a mille-feuille or a delicate flaky
croissant? There’s still a petite-bon-coin for every taste.

But if you're lucky enough to spend time outside of Île de France, you'll get
to know the quaint villages scattered throughout the country. Lying between
these fairytale villages are expanses of vineyards and farmland, with bucolic
scenes of grazing sheep, cows, and goats supplying the milk for the astounding
variety of cheese from small farms, as surprising as discovering aisle after
aisle of glistening pink bottles of rosé in a Provençal grocery store, or the
sheer number of fresh-caught fish options you'd find in the Basque Country.

It wasn't long ago that on any given day, a visit to one of these villages one
could forget which century they were in when wandering around the market on
cobbled squares: rounds and blocks of soft and hard cheeses, wafts of buttery
scented baked goods alongside artfully stacked piles heirloom vegetables, jars
of golden honey, bouquets of dried herbes, cured meats, and fresh eggs of all
sizes and colors. Sadly, now you're just as likely to stumble upon a table of
imported produce and cheap goods from the other side of the globe. More and
more farmers are squeezed by strict, unattainable permitting and regulations,
and the small farms are disappearing as fast as your collection of wine you
meant to keep for a special occasion.

The first time I went to a superstore in France, I was crushed by what felt
like a bad copy of Costco: giant boxes of Kellogg's cereal translated into
French were still just overprocessed junk food: Coco Chanel replaced by
Cocopuffs; aisle upon aisle of ultra-processed "gouter" for kids. Faster than
a snobby Parisian waiter tosses change at a tourist’s table, it dashed my
fantasy of French children eating only hunks of fresh baguette with slabs of
cultured butter while sipping chocolat chaud. American-style junk food has
spread like a disease all over the world. Don't worry, there are shops selling
only local produce, but farmers are abandoning ship. Their fields, once green
swaths that not only grew food crops and pastured livestock, but also served
as fire breaks, are vanishing. Maritime pine, Scotch broom, and other invasive
brush have crept in, and with the hotter temperatures, they've quickly become
tinder boxes now going up in terrifying, explosive flames. The precious French
terroir, so much a part of the very fabric and foundation of the culture, was
something I (an American, suburb-raised kid) had only imagined in young dreams
of living in an old farmhouse, raising food for my family. It has been swapped
for fuel for megafires.

During my time in Cap Ferret, I admired the pine forests from paths leading to
the silky blonde sand beaches, passageways to a Renoir scene of beach
umbrellas, topless sunbathers, and children frolicking in the waves,
modernized only by surfers and kite surfers making the most of endless French
summer vacation time. I breathed deep their rich odor, especially strong on
the hottest days, before I learned these trees weren't native at all: planted
by Napoléon III, following in his uncle’s footsteps, to keep the dunes from
blowing around and transforming the marshlands of yore into giant swaths of
forest. Behind the rows and rows of pines lie the endless dunes of les landes,
before the dreamy waters of the Atlantic, wild and cold in winter, but
inviting the other six months of the year. These same trees have now popped up
between houses that once stood on empty lots, shading them in their new wooded
settings through the hot summer.

So, what are the French eating now? The same produce as we Americans, imported
from South America and Mexico. Though the French government promises to
tighten regulations on imports, the big grocery stores are filled with little
else: those wee sweet grapes, Nantes carrots, and Rouge d'hiver pumpkins are
replaced by the same things we've come to expect year-round in the US: peppers
and tomatoes, eggplants and tropical fruits, and anything the home cook
desires any month of the year.

And just like that, those fantasy ideas about France are going up in flames
along with Napoléon's pines, while the charming houses of southwest France lie
in piles of ash and red roof tiles, ready to be replaced by little houses made
of ticky-tacky.
